title: A cooler route to school
paragraphs: At Meranti Secondary School, many students walked from the bus stop along a 600-metre route with little shelter. During the dry season, student council members noticed that the open section beside the sports field felt much hotter than the tree-lined lane near the library. They began a heat-mapping project to compare conditions along the route and identify places where shade could make the walk more comfortable.

Over two weeks, teams measured three fixed points: the unshaded asphalt beside the sports field, a covered walkway and the tree-lined lane. They took readings at 7.15 a.m., 12.30 p.m. and 3.30 p.m. using the same sensor, held one metre above the ground for thirty seconds. Rain days were excluded because wet surfaces become temporarily cooler and would distort the comparison.

The midday readings showed the clearest difference. On average, the exposed asphalt surface was eight degrees Celsius warmer than the surface under the trees, while the covered walkway fell between the two. The morning gap was much smaller. Students also counted pedestrians, but they did not ask people why they chose a particular route. Their report therefore treated the temperature readings and pedestrian counts as separate sets of evidence.

Using the measurements, the students proposed shade sails near the main gate, a drinking-water refill point and new trees beside the sports field. The town council approved a six-week trial of shade sails at the main gate. It postponed tree planting because drainage pipes beneath the verge first required an engineering survey, and it deferred the refill point because of maintenance costs.

During the trial, the surface beneath the sails averaged five degrees Celsius cooler than nearby exposed pavement at midday. The number of people using the shaded entrance also increased. However, the report explicitly stated that the counts could not prove the lower temperature caused the increase: an examination schedule and a bus-stop relocation had also changed during the trial. The students published their readings, measurement times and excluded days so another group could examine the conclusion.
